Odious

OH-dee-us -- from Latin odium ('hatred'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Odious is arousing or deserving intense dislike or hatred.

Nobody on the crew wanted the odious job of cleaning the grease trap after the dinner rush.

Worked Example

Even the landlord's own lawyer admitted the eviction notice's wording was needlessly odious, practically taunting the tenants on their way out.

That kind of behavior or task that makes people recoil in disgust or resentment is exactly what odious describes.

How Odious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

unpleasant

unpleasant: not enjoyable or agreeable in any way

repugnant

repugnant: causing intense disgust or distaste

Antonyms

delightful

delightful: very pleasing and enjoyable

charming

charming: attractive and pleasant in manner

How Strong Is It? — unpleasant → odious → repugnant

unpleasant vs. odious

unpleasant vs. odious: Unpleasant is much milder than odious: a waiting room can smell faintly unpleasant, but an odious plan stirs intense dislike, even hatred, in everyone who hears it.

repugnant vs. odious

repugnant vs. odious: Repugnant is harsher than odious: an odious scheme earns strong dislike, but profiting from a disaster is repugnant — it goes further, provoking outright disgust.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Odious traces back to Latin odium, 'hatred' -- the same idea survives in the rare English word odium itself, but the root doesn't extend cleanly into other everyday words, so odious is best learned as its own strong, standalone term for something hatred-worthy.

Use the root in a new word: odium

Use the root in a new word: odium: Historians still debate why the emperor was held in such odium by his own generals.

Root Check

Word Choice

Odious usually describes behavior, tasks, or qualities that provoke real disgust or resentment -- a milder, more common word like 'unpleasant' works for everyday annoyances, while odious is reserved for something genuinely hate-worthy. Contrast this with maleficent, taught earlier in this unit, which describes active evil intent rather than simple disgust.
